[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya Chen from Redwood, AE. We'll get started in a sec, just wanna confirm folks can hear me.
[00:08] Aisha: Yep, loud and clear. Hi Maya, hi Liam.
[00:12] Carlos: Good afternoon.
[00:15] Liam: Hey all, Liam O'Connor on the Seattle side, RD for infra.
[00:20] Dana: Dana here, FinOps.
[00:22] Maya: Great. Quick agenda: 1) usage and runway numbers from Kepler, 2) cost options—hosted vs dedicated committed, 3) reliability and incident triage, 4) pilot stress test and next steps. Sound right?
[00:34] Aisha: Yep that's perfect. We're hoping to decide on whether to commit for Q1 by end of month.
[00:39] Maya: Understood. Carlos, do you wanna start with the high-level prod signals?
[00:43] Carlos: Sure. Over the last 90 days we've seen a 2.5x increase in chat requests, peak hour 1.8k rps in our EU region. Average token per request around 420, but some session flows spike to 3k tokens. We're worried about tail latency. We also hit a few 503s last week during a deploy.
[01:06] Liam: When you say 503s, is that from upstream timeouts or from model-side? Any stack traces?
[01:11] Carlos: It's a mixture—kube pod churn combined with a retry loop in our client that created bursts. We instrumented a histogram, saw p95 jump from 180ms to 900ms on two incidents.
[01:22] Maya: Thanks; that helps. From Redwood perspective the burst profile matches a cold-spot where your autoscaling didn't spin up enough dedicated workers—if you go hosted there's more transparent immediate capacity, but dedicated committed capacity will give you predictable throughput and lower per-token cost.
[01:38] Aisha: Right, but our security team prefers private deployments or VPC connections. We need to know KMS integration and audit logs—Dana is pushing that.
[01:46] Dana: Yep. Also want to understand the unit economics. If we commit, how much can we drop per-token costs, and what's the downside if usage dips?
[01:55] Maya: Good question. We prepared a committed pricing model where at 1.2M tokens/day committed for Q1 you see about 22% reduction vs pay-as-you-go (hosted). We can share a sensitivity table. There are step-down tiers and a decommitment window but it's not zero-risk—there's an overage rate and a small ramp clause.
[02:14] Carlos: Could you send the table after the call? Also curious about quantization—do you have model variants that we can serve to cut cost but keep latency?
[02:22] Liam: Yes, we have quantized variants and automatic fallback routing. In practice we recommend a staged rollout: start with a 4-bit quantized model for non-critical heavy endpoints and keep fp16 for low-latency flows. The runtime supports KV cache warming so frequent-chat sessions don't re-gen the whole context. That usually preserves p95 while saving tokens.
[02:40] Aisha: Warming KV cache—how soon does it populate? Our sessions are often new users each time.
[02:46] Liam: If you have a stable prefix or assistant prompts, that warms quickly. For brand-new users it's less effective but batching and smart routing still cut costs. We can also suggest prompt compression strategies.
[02:56] Dana: On the financial side, what happens if we commit and then usage drops by 40%? Is there a true downscale?
[03:03] Maya: We include a right-sizing clause—partial credit against next quarter if usage falls under 60% of committed baseline, with a cap. We'll put exact terms in the spreadsheet.
[03:12] Carlos: Sounds fair. Let's talk reliability. The 503s—how do we prevent these? We want playbooks.
[03:18] Liam: On our side we recommend two mitigations: 1) increase burst capacity allowance for peak windows (we can configure auto-burst up to a defined throughput), 2) circuit-breaker client-side to avoid retry storms. We also offer canary routing and automatic fallback to smaller context models if memory pressure rises.
[03:36] Aisha: Canary routing is appealing. Does fall back to a smaller model mean worse results? We have quality bar checks.
[03:43] Liam: There is some degradation, yes. We typically tie that to an eval set so we can quantify QoQ drift. Redwood Optimize can run evals against the two variants and show delta.
[03:52] Dana: Please include delta numbers in the price/sla doc. Finance needs a cost vs quality delta to approve the commit.
[03:58] Maya: Absolutely. We'll include a chart: expected token cost savings vs expected QA drop for the quantized path.
[04:04] [05:00] Speaker 1: (muffled) sorry lost you for a sec 
[05:05] Maya: no worries—back.
[05:08] Aisha: Quick question on auditing: do we get per-request audit logs and the ability to forward them to our Splunk?
[05:14] Maya: Yes, we can stream audit logs to your logging endpoint, or you can pull them from the console. We also support SAML SSO and RBAC for team access. For key management we support AWS KMS and customer-managed key rotation. We'll attach the SOC2 package and KMS integration notes to the follow-up.
[05:29] Dana: That helps. Also curious—what's the typical latency difference if we move from hosted Redwood to a Private VPC deployment on our cloud?
[05:37] Liam: It depends on egress and the proximity of the model pool. Private VPC can shave overhead for control-plane traffic and meet security requirements, but you need to run the inference nodes close to your frontend. In our benchmarks, colocated VPC deployments had median latency comparable to hosted, sometimes slightly better, but operational burden is higher if you self-manage.
[05:55] Carlos: We prefer minimal ops work. If dedicated hosted can meet our SLA, that's ideal.
[06:00] Maya: Our Dedicated offering gives the committed capacity + Redwood-managed infra. For many customers that's the sweet spot: lower cost, predictable throughput, and you keep the control plane connectivity via VPC peering if needed.
[06:11] Aisha: Ok. On pilot stress tests—how should we design those to be realistic to our traffic?
[06:16] Liam: We recommend two runs: 1) a throughput run matching your peak hour 1.8k rps scaled to full token distribution, 2) a spike test where we create a burst with high-token sessions to validate autoscale and canary fallback. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and error rates. We can also include a mem-leak check for long sessions.
[06:34] Maya: We'll need your anonymized traffic sample. Aisha, can you share that?
[06:37] Aisha: Yes I can. We'll scrub PII and remove any PHI—should be ready in 48 hours.
[06:42] Dana: From procurement, we need to see committed price vs pay-as-you-go scenario for 6-month and 12-month terms, also cancellation terms.
[06:50] Maya: We'll put a two-tab spreadsheet: 6-month and 12-month sensitivity. Also include a blended per-token cost and expected monthly invoice delta.
[06:59] [07:30] Carlos: Also can we get a sample SLA? We have internal uptime targets and would like to map them to Redwood's credits.
[07:35] Maya: Yes, SLA doc linked in the deck. We'll highlight p95 latency SLOs, uptime, and credits bands.
[07:41] Aisha: Tough question—what about competitor lock-in? If we want to move models or run hybrid, how portable is the setup?
[07:48] Liam: We focus on portability: model formats are standard (ONNX/transformer checkpoints) and your prompts are your assets. If you want a self-hosted appliance later, we support a private deployment package. We can also export audit logs and traffic metrics.
[07:59] Dana: Good. One more finance nit: if we commit, do we need to pre-pay? Our policy prefers net-30 billing, not large pre-pay.
[08:06] Maya: There's some flexibility—monthly invoicing is possible for larger commitments with credit check; for initial pilot we recommend pay-as-you-go or a small committed deposit. We'll outline options.
[08:18] Carlos: Let's talk timeline. We want to finalize commit decision by 01/31. Can Redwood have pricing and SOC2 docs before then?
[08:26] Maya: Yes, we'll deliver pricing and SOC2 by 01/25. Benchmarks scheduled for 01/28.
[08:31] Aisha: Sounds tight but doable.
[08:33] Liam: For the benchmark, we'll need an API key and a staging endpoint. Aisha, do you have a staging cluster we can push load from or should we run from Redwood side?
[08:41] Aisha: We can provide a staging endpoint and API key. We'll also provide the anonymized traffic.
[08:45] Liam: Great. We'll run both hosted and a dedicated-config simulation so you can compare p95 and cost.
[08:51] Dana: Please include tokenization breakdown in the results—how many input vs generated tokens, we track those differently in our billing model.
[08:58] Maya: We'll add that to the benchmark output.
[09:01] [09:30] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[09:33] Carlos: Real quick—on RBAC, can we restrict model rollout permissions to only a small group? We need guardrails.
[09:39] Maya: Yes, the Console supports role-based permissions and can lock model rollouts behind approvals. We'll show a screenshot in the follow-up.
[09:47] Aisha: Okay recapping next steps?
[09:50] Maya: Sure. 1) Redwood to send pricing & SOC2/KMS docs by 2026-01-25. 2) Kepler to provide anonymized 7-day traffic sample and staging endpoint by 2026-01-24. 3) Redwood SE to run stress run on 2026-01-28 and share results within 72 hours. 4) Kepler FinOps confirms budget runway by 2026-01-29.
[10:12] Dana: I'll escalate internally.
[10:14] Carlos: One last question: do you have guidance on prompt engineering to reduce tokens without hurting UX?
[10:20] Liam: Yes—prompt compaction, templating, removing redundant context, and server-side summarization. We can run an evaluation set and show before/after token counts.
[10:30] Aisha: That might be an easy win; please include sample before/after.
[10:34] Maya: We'll include a separate mini-run for prompt compression.
[10:38] [40:00] Maya: Alright if there's nothing else, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the sheet and links.
[40:08] Aisha: Thanks, talk soon.
[40:11] Carlos: Thanks all.
[40:13] Dana: Bye.
